title: Infra playbook: GPU fleet, capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules, CI/CD and runbooks (2026 ops guide)
author: Marco Nguyen
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook consolidates operational best practices for managing Redwood Inference's GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines, and common infra runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate the serving runtime and GPU-backed clusters.

Scope: Covers multi-cloud account structure, VPC design patterns, Terraform module conventions, CI/CD build & release patterns for infra modules, capacity forecasting methodology, automated scaling playbooks, and incident/runbook steps for GPU-related failures. Not a substitute for team-level runbooks that reference customer-specific private deployments.

Goals and SLOs

- Keep GPU request P95 scheduling latency < 150 ms for dedicated pools.
- Maintain cluster utilization target 70-85% for cost-efficiency; trigger scale-up if sustained > 85% for 30m.
- Provision headroom: minimum 10% spare capacity across regions for burst traffic.
- Reduce manual scaling events to < 1 per month per region.

Ownership and contacts

- Infra Platform (primary): infra-platform@redwood.example.com
- GPU Fleet Owners: Rafael Ortiz (gpufleet@redwood.example.com)
- Cloud Accounts & Networking: Leah Kim (cloudops@redwood.example.com)
- CI/CD & IaC: Marco Nguyen (iac-builds@redwood.example.com)
- Pager rotations: see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/pager-rotations

Architecture overview

- GPU pools are organized as: hosted/dedicated/private lanes -> region -> instance-family (A100s / H100s / L4s).
- Control plane services run in the management AWS account; serving nodes are in region accounts that are readonly to control plane.
- Terraform modules (infra/*) are published in the internal registry and versioned with semver. Module types include: vpc, subnet, k8s-cluster, gpu-node-pool, iam-roles, networking-peering, ebs-storage, monitoring

Capacity planning and forecasting process

1) Monthly forecast run (owners: GPU Fleet, Infra Platform)
   - Inputs: 30/90/365-day rolling usage curves, committed customers, expected launches.
   - Output: target nodes by region and instance-family, purchase/commit recommendations.

2) Thresholds and automated triggers:

| Metric | Warning | Action |
|---|---:|---|
| Cluster utilization (avg) | 70% | Evaluate autoscaling policies (informing runbook) |
| Cluster utilization (sustained) | 85% for 30m | Autoscale + send capacity augmentation request to procurement |
| Queue depth (pending pods) | > 10% of capacity | Trigger instant burst capacity (hotpool) |
| Preemption rate (spot) | > 5% | Move non-critical workloads to on-demand slots |

3) Reserve strategy: maintain 10% cold reserve (idle but available nodes) during business hours; 5% overnight.

Cloud accounts & networking patterns

- Account topology: management-account (control plane), shared-services, production-region-accounts (one per region), dev-test accounts.
- Account naming: redwood-{env}-{region} (e.g., redwood-prod-us-west-2).
- VPC layout: one primary VPC per region-account for serving, segmented into public/ingress and private/service subnets. Use /20 CIDRs to allow growth; record CIDR allocations in the central IPAM spreadsheet.
- Peering/Transit: use Transit Gateway for cross-account, cross-region routing. Explicit peering only for short-lived test networks.
- Networking security: default deny via NSGs/firewalls; allow kube API from management CIDR and Bastion sessions via SSO jump hosts.

Common networking configs (table)

| Component | Default | Rationale |
| VPC CIDR | /20 | Growth buffer for pods and services |
| Subnet sizing | /24 | Reserve for node pools with multiple instance types |
| Load balancer idle timeout | 120s | Prevent premature connection closes during streaming responses |
| Egress NAT gateway | Managed NAT | Centralized egress/egress tagging for billing |

Terraform / IaC modules & conventions

- Repository layout (mono-repo): infra/modules/*, infra/environments/*, infra/pipelines/*
- Module conventions:
  - All modules must have: inputs.tf (schema), outputs.tf, README.md with examples, tests/ (unit plan tests), changelog.md.
  - Modules are immutable once published; bugfixes increment patch version and release notes updated.
  - Use module source pinning in environment stacks (registry+version).

- Example module usage (snippet):

  module "gpu_node_pool" {
    source  = "registry.internal.redwood/infra/gpu-node-pool"
    version = "~> 2.3"

    cluster_id       = module.k8s_cluster.id
    instance_family  = "nvidia-a100-40gb"
    desired_capacity = 16
    min_capacity     = 4
    max_capacity     = 64
  }

- Secrets and state:
  - Use remote state with encryption + workspace per environment (s3 + DynamoDB for locking).
  - Do not store secrets in tfstate; reference secrets from the secrets module which reads from KMS-protected AWS Secret Manager or Vault.

CI/CD and build patterns for infra modules

- Pipeline stages (per module change):
  1) Lint & fmt (tflint, tfsec quick-scan)
  2) Unit plan (terraform init/plan) using a dry run workspace
  3) Integration smoke (apply to ephemeral test account and run validation helm chart)
  4) Approval gate (peer-review + security review for networking/iam changes)
  5) Promote module release (publish to registry)
  6) Environment plan/apply via environment pipeline (with manual approval for prod)

- Safeguards and reviewers:
  - Any change that modifies kubernetes node pool sizing, instance family, or cross-account IAM must have a security reviewer and a capacity reviewer.
  - Prod applies require two approvers if change touches node pools or networking.

Runbooks and common procedures

1) GPU node degraded (high OOMs / driver crashes)
   - Confirm alerts: driver-crash-rate > 1% and node-restarts > 3 in 15m.
   - Steps: cordon node; drain non-critical pods; collect logs (/var/log/nvidia*, dmesg, kubelet logs); escalate to GPU Fleet team; if driver bug suspected, roll driver via daemonset with canary 1 node then 10% -> 100%.

2) Sudden capacity pressure
   - Trigger: pending pod queue > 10% or sustained utilization > 85% for 30m.
   - Steps: verify autoscaler metrics; if autoscaler failing, run manual scale: terraform apply with increased desired_capacity; if quota limits hit, open support ticket with cloud provider and activate hotpool (pre-warmed on-demand nodes).

3) Network partition between control plane and region
   - Verify transit gateway BGP/route table; check VPC reachability with aws ec2 reachability tests; failover: shift routing for read-only telemetry to backup region and reduce traffic by enabling degraded serving mode (route-by-policy to cheaper variants).

4) Patch and upgrade node pools
   - Upgrade strategy: canary -> rolling batch -> validation -> promote. Default batch size is 10% for critical pools or 1 node for small pools. Always run release in dev then staging before prod.

Day-2 operations checklist

- Weekly: review cluster utilization dashboards, pending pods trend, preemption incidents.
- Monthly: run capacity forecast job, reconcile IaC drift, rotate credentials for service accounts referenced by modules.
- Quarterly: run disaster recovery drill (region failover) and review runbook effectiveness.

Monitoring, alerts and dashboards

- Dashboards: GPU Fleet Overview, Region Utilization, Node Health, Pod Scheduling Latency, Networking Errors.
- Key alerts (examples):
  - GPU node kernel panic (sev1) -> page oncall
  - Scheduling latency P95 > 150 ms (sev2) -> page infra-platform (Slack + ticket)
  - Autoscaler failures (API errors) -> page infra-platform & iac-builds

Automation and tooling

- Automation components: capacity-forecast (cron job), hotpool-manager (lambda/controller), tf-plan-bot (reports PR plan diffs), infra-compliance-checker (pre-merge checks).
- CLI snippets:
  - View node pools: kubectl get nodes -l nodepool=gpupool-a100 -o wide
  - Trigger terraform plan for prod env: infra/pipelines/prod-plan.sh --env prod --module gpu-node-pool

Rollout and migration checklist for instance-family changes

1) Validate performance profile in benchmarking cluster (latency, throughput, cost per token).
2) Publish module change with new instance_family flag and default off.
3) Test canary with 1-2 nodes in staging for 48h.
4) Gradual rollout 10% -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring for regen errors and latency regression.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Force a hotpool scale (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://controlplane.internal.redwood/api/v1/hotpool/scale -d '{"region":"us-west-2","instance_family":"nvidia-a100-40gb","desired":8}'

- Terraform state unlock (only if absolutely necessary):
  aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name infra-terraform-locks --key '{"LockID": {"S": "workspace-prod-gpu-node-pool"}}'

- Quick diagnostic checklist to collect for postmortems:
  - cluster-id, region, nodepool name, node IDs
  - prometheus query results (utilization history), kube events, driver logs, cloud provider events

Related pages and references

- infra-gpu-fleet-capacity-ci-cd-iac-playbook-2026 (team-wiki)
- infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (terraform-and-iac)
- eng-sre/runbooks/gpu-incident-sops

Document maintenance

- Owner: Marco Nguyen (IaC & pipelines)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or after any Sev1 related to GPU capacity/networking.

If you find missing details (example: updated CIDR allocations, new module versions, or contact rotations) please file an update PR to this page or contact the owner team.
